agentCan: Run the authorization/token endpoints against each customer instance once the registry record exists
Detect refresh failure and re-prompt for authorization gracefully

approval.cost: No fee for OAuth configuration, Store certification, or partner program participation is stated in the documentation read
approval.trigger: OAuth itself: no ServiceNow (vendor-side) review or approval exists. The only approvers are the customer's instance admin, who creates the registry record, and the authorizing user, who consents at oauth_auth.do. There is no ServiceNow-side submission, review queue, cap, or fee for creating OAuth endpoints in an instance; the object doesn't exist until the customer's admin creates it, and it never leaves that instance. Gating is entirely customer-controlled, per instance, and usually entangled with the customer's internal change/security process (outside ServiceNow's documentation). Store distribution (optional, separate track): to publish a scoped app to the ServiceNow Store, product documentation states the prerequisites are: 'Create an application within a private application scope. Join the Technology Partner Program. Have the application certified.' And: 'Applications in the global scope cannot be published to the ServiceNow Store.' Certification runs through the Store Publisher Portal with two tracks: App review (Design Document and Test Plan with results, plus a customer-facing Installation Guide; the team inspects 'the security and performance of the app', platform stability and UX, the installation process, and architecture/best practices) and Listing review (marketing documentation/demo videos checked for accuracy and branding). Only partner-program (Build Partner) participants can list apps. The official App Publisher blog states the timeline: 'Certification, from design complete and submission for certification to ready for publishing on the store, typically requires 3-5 weeks. It is very possible to complete certification in a matter of days; likewise, it may take longer than 5 weeks.' This applies ONLY to Store certification.
approval.wait: OAuth: none (no vendor review). Store certification: 'typically requires 3-5 weeks' (stated, official blog)

blockers.detail: Credentials, redirect URLs, scopes, and token lifespans are all per customer instance. A SaaS cannot pre-register anything; onboarding N customers means N admin-guided registry setups with N different Client ID/Secret pairs, and non-prod vs prod instances of the SAME customer are separate again.
blockers.howToClear: Build an admin-guided, per-instance onboarding flow and a credential store keyed by instance URL.
blockers.title: Per-instance everything

blockers.detail: 'Role required: admin': delegated/non-admin users generally cannot create the record, so connection setup depends on the busiest person in the customer's org. Nothing the vendor does can shortcut this.
blockers.howToClear: Give the customer's admin a complete, copy-paste-ready setup packet (redirect URL, requested grant type, scope guidance) to minimize their effort.
blockers.title: The admin is the gatekeeper

blockers.detail: Pre-Zurich instances use System OAuth > Application Registry ('Create an OAuth API endpoint for external clients'); Zurich+ instances use the Machine Identity Console inbound-integration flow. Instructions written for one will not match the other's screens.
blockers.howToClear: Maintain both instruction sets and ask the customer which release their instance runs before sending setup steps.
blockers.title: Version fork in the setup UX

alternatives: Resource Owner Password Credentials grant (supported as an inbound integration type; used by many vendors with a service account's username/password; simpler for headless sync, weaker security posture)

Client Credentials grant (machine-to-machine with no interactive user; the registry record designates an OAuth Application User whose roles the token inherits; not on by default for inbound use: an admin must first create the system property glide.oauth.inbound.client.credential.grant_type.enabled = true and add the OAuth Application User / Default Grant Type fields to the form layout)
Third-party ID token (inbound integrations that accept an external IdP's ID token)
Shipping a scoped app through the ServiceNow Store (distribution alternative; the in-instance OAuth pieces still register per instance, see Approval)
flavor.recommended: An Authorization Code grant registry record / inbound integration, created per customer instance, with a dedicated integration user
flavor.why: ServiceNow has no centralized developer-portal app program for OAuth. The OAuth object lives inside each customer's own instance and is created by that instance's administrator: classically an OAuth application registry record ('OAuth Entity') under System OAuth > Application Registry, created with 'Create an OAuth API endpoint for external clients' (the instance auto-generates the Client ID and Client Secret; the secret field can be left blank to have the instance auto-generate it). From the Zurich release, the current object is an Inbound Integration configured in the Machine Identity Console (All > Inbound integrations > New integration), where the admin picks a grant type (separate configuration pages exist for Authorization code, Resource owner password credentials, Client Credentials, and third-party ID token). ServiceNow acts purely as the authorization server of that one instance: endpoints are per-instance (<instance>.service-now.com/oauth_auth.do and /oauth_token.do). Tokens act with the authorizing user's permissions, so a dedicated integration user whose roles/ACLs bound the token is the safe pattern.

humanMust: (Customer instance admin) Verify the OAuth plugin is active on the instance
(Customer instance admin) Create the registry record / inbound integration with the vendor's exact redirect URL, and set auth scopes and token lifespans
(Customer instance admin) Retrieve the Client ID and Client Secret (click the lock icon to reveal the secret) and hand them, plus the instance URL, to the vendor securely
(Vendor, in advance) Supply the exact redirect URL the admin must register
name: ServiceNow
nuances: Scope semantics are coarse and admin-defined: unlike providers with a fixed scope catalog, ServiceNow auth scopes are created by the admin and mapped to API lists; if 'Allow access only to APIs in selected scope' is left off, the token inherits whatever the authorizing user's ACLs/API policies permit, so effective permissions are a property of the USER, not your app. Admins can also enable 'Enforce token restriction' (tokens confined to APIs named in REST API Access Policies); token format can be JWT or Opaque (JWKS served at api/now/oauth/jwks; 'The rotated (inactive keys) from jwks response is removed after 105 days default').

Token lifespan is the customer's setting, not yours: if an admin shortens the refresh-token lifespan on the registry record, your connections silently start expiring at that cadence. The documented user-context scope for the authorization flow is 'useraccount'.

Redirect-URL matching quirk (classic registry): 'The instance matches the URL of the incoming request to one of the redirect URLs. If no match is made, the instance uses the first redirect URL', so a mis-ordered registry can send codes to the wrong environment (e.g. staging) without an error.

Instances can require the OAuth state parameter (system property-controlled); clients that omit state may fail authorization against hardened instances ('Missing state parameter in the request'). Store one-way door: an app must be in a private scope to be publishable, so deciding to distribute via the Store after building in the global scope means re-packaging.
prerequisites: A customer instance admin ('Role required: admin')
The vendor's exact redirect URL supplied to the admin in advance
A dedicated integration user in the customer's instance with least-privilege roles

steps.detail: The admin verifies the OAuth plugin is active (System Definition > Plugins). Classic path: System OAuth > Application Registry > New > 'Create an OAuth API endpoint for external clients'. Zurich+ path: Machine Identity Console > Inbound integrations > New integration, selecting the grant type (e.g. 'OAuth, Authorization code grant'). 'Role required: admin.'

links.label: Configure an OAuth authorization code grant (Zurich)

steps.title: (Customer admin) Create the OAuth record in the instance

steps.detail: Name; Redirect URL (the vendor's callback); optional Logo URL (shown on the consent/approval page) and Comments. Client ID is auto-generated; the Client Secret may be left blank for auto-generation. Optionally create/select an Auth scope listing the APIs to limit authorization to, and adjust token lifespans (defaults: access 1800 seconds, refresh 8,640,000 seconds).
steps.title: (Customer admin) Configure the record

steps.detail: Reopen the record, click the lock icon to reveal the Client Secret, and copy the Client ID and Client Secret. Enter the instance URL + credentials into the SaaS's connection form. (For client-credentials setups, the admin additionally adds the OAuth Application User and Default Grant Type fields to the form layout and selects a least-privilege user.)
steps.title: (Customer admin) Retrieve and hand off the credentials

steps.detail: Redirect the authorizing user to https://<instance>.service-now.com/oauth_auth.do with the client ID, redirect URI, and scope ('useraccount'); the user logs into the instance and approves (logo shown on the approval page). Exchange the returned code at https://<instance>.service-now.com/oauth_token.do.
steps.title: Run the authorization flow against the instance

steps.detail: Within the refresh-token lifespan (default 100 days), exchange the refresh token at oauth_token.do for a new access token without user interaction. Once the window elapses, the user must re-authorize.
steps.title: Refresh within the 100-day window

tagline: ServiceNow has no central OAuth app to register: each customer's instance admin creates the OAuth record inside their own instance (defaults: 30-minute access tokens, 100-day refresh tokens) and hands you the credentials. The only ServiceNow-side review anywhere is the optional Store certification, typically 3 to 5 weeks.
